extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP counsel, judges, and law students studying Federal Circuit patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Federal Circuit standards and legal criteria for patent litigation issues including pleading infringement, claim construction (including at the motion-to-dismiss stage), printed matter, inducement, capability to infringe, and doctrine of equivalents. Useful as a reference for litigators and courts applying these doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: License scope determination at motion to dismiss
rubrics_metrics.description: A license granted by agreement extends only to the specific transactions described (e.g., 'transactions involving activation of, or adding value to, an account'); not every act that infringes will necessarily be licensed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A district court may err by finding a license covers all alleged infringement based solely on limited complaint allegations and attachments; factual issues (e.g., whether the license terminated or was amended) may preclude resolution on a motion to dismiss and should be developed at the district-court fact stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for pleading categorizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit reviews de novo a district court's categorization of complaint allegations as well-pleaded factual (to be credited) versus conclusory (not credited) at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts independently decide whether allegations are factual or conclusory when reviewing dismissals for failure to state a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of pleading patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff is 'not required to plead infringement on an element-by-element basis'—a complaint need only place the accused infringer on notice of what activity is being accused of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed infringement theory and claim charts that provide fair notice will survive a motion to dismiss, particularly for simpler technologies. Courts should not resolve contested factual disputes about operational roles on a motion to dismiss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading indirect (induced) infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff need not identify a specific customer induced to infringe; references to product brochures, promotional materials, or other marketplace communications can support a plausible inference that at least one direct infringer exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations of intent (e.g., providing product support, instructions, or promotional materials) may suffice to plead inducement at the pleading stage; combine factual marketplace evidence with label/communications to plead specific intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court may construe claims when deciding a motion to dismiss if the construction is based solely on intrinsic evidence; this is 'proper and routine' and is not procedurally erroneous even if done without a separate Markman proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have wide latitude in how they conduct claim construction; relying on intrinsic evidence alone to interpret claim scope at 12(b)(6) is permissible and reviewed de novo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting plural terms and 'group' language
rubrics_metrics.description: Plural terms (like 'group' or plural nouns) are presumptive indicators but not dispositive that multiple items are required; the meaning may be 'one or more' depending on context and specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim interpretation must go beyond ordinary/commonsense meaning where appropriate—consider specification, prosecution history, and extrinsic evidence; do not assume 'group' requires 'two or more' without deeper analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: When specification/'present invention' language limits claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a specification consistently describes an aspect (e.g., 'pre-fetching' advertisements) as part of the 'present invention,' that language can support a limiting claim construction tying the claim term to that aspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the written description uniformly associates the claimed term with a particular feature and consult prosecution history (e.g., applicant statements) that may confirm a limiting meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not read exemplary embodiments into claims ('for example' is non-limiting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language in the specification that presents an embodiment 'for example' indicates that the embodiment is exemplary and should not be read as a required limitation into the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid importing specific location, structure, or other embodiment details (e.g., requiring colocation at a cable-TV head-end) unless the claim language or clear intrinsic evidence mandates such a limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter doctrine two-step test
rubrics_metrics.description: First determine whether the limitation is directed to printed matter (i.e., claims the content/information being communicated). Second, if it is printed matter, determine whether the informational content has a functional or structural relationship to the substrate such that it should be given patentable weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The act of communication or the fact that information exists is not itself 'content'—claims to 'encrypted communications' or 'program code' without claiming particular content may not be 'printed matter.' Apply the two-step test before denying patentable weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importing narrow technical limitations absent supporting claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not narrow a claim term to a particular technical implementation (e.g., 'back channel' limited to 'fixed band of frequencies or time slots') when nothing in the claim language requires that limitation and the specification shows broader embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification describes both fixed and dynamic embodiments, the exemplified (fixed) embodiment is not a constraint unless the claim unambiguously requires it; avoid construing each subphrase in isolation if dependent on a rejected construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB implicit claim construction principle
rubrics_metrics.description: If the outcome of the Board's analysis effectively establishes the scope and boundaries of a claim term, the Board has construed the claim—even if it says it did not 'engage in claim construction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate review will treat such determinations as claim construction and assess whether the Board's implicit construction is legally correct based on claim language and intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capability-to-infringe / 'reasonably capable' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An accused device may be found to infringe if it is 'reasonably capable' of satisfying the claim limitations; a product that is 'readily configurable to infringe' can meet the capability standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But the patentee must prove the capability with evidence that alleged infringing functionality is accessible to customers (not only to manufacturer technicians or experts), and show actual configurability—not mere testimony that someone 'could have' configured it without proof that customers can or did.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced infringement pleading standard (knowledge + affirmative inducement)
rubrics_metrics.description: To state a claim for induced infringement, a patent owner must plausibly allege (1) direct infringement by a third party and (2) that the alleged infringer affirmatively induced that infringement with knowledge that the induced acts constituted patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market communications (press releases, websites, labeling) combined with contextual facts (e.g., describing the product as 'generic' to a brand whose majority sales are for the patented use) can support a plausible claim of inducement even where a skinny-label/carve-out exists; clarity and consistency in a generic manufacturer's communications are important to avoid inducement liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents (DOE) evidentiary sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A jury verdict finding infringement under the doctrine of equivalents can be set aside if the evidentiary record is inadequate to support equivalence for the point of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court must assess whether evidence supports that the accused product performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result for the claimed point of novelty; insufficient evidence permits judgment as a matter of law of noninfringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting claim modifiers such as 'single'
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifiers like 'single' in a claim (e.g., 'identifying a single biomolecule') should be given their ordinary meaning in context and can require capability to perform the claimed function on one item alone (i.e., examine one molecule by itself rather than an ensemble).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification's emphasis on the modifier can confirm that inclusion of a word like 'single' was intended to require that specific capability; look to specification and ordinary meaning to resolve disputes.
